newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Bertie Ahern -- Ireland's new premier.
newsitem.headline: Bertie Ahern -- Ireland's new premier.

text.p: Bertie Ahern cast himself as the people's choice in Ireland's national elections but the people only gave his Fianna Fail party and its Progressive Democrat allies the mandate for a minority government.
Long groomed by the party barons to become Prime Minister, the 45-year-old Ahern will have to continue the pursuit of power with the help of independent legislators.
He will need the reputation he has built up in a lifetime career in politics as a conciliator to manage the parliamentary arithmetic to serve his full five-year term.
His campaign strategy was rooted in Fianna Fail's belief that it is the true voice of all Irish people with a populist appeal to small businessmen, farmer and entrepreneur alike.
Ahern shook tens of thousands of hands and kissed babies, belles and grandmothers in an election campaign the like of which Ireland had not seen in seven decades.

His campaign poster, showing a thoughtful Ahern listening to an unseen audience, promised "People before Politics" and vowed to tackle crime, tax and, Northern Ireland, the lingering headache only 80 miles (120 km) from Dublin.

Ahern has promised to be the voice of the province's Catholic pro-Irish nationalist minority but to distance himself from its self-styled champions, Sinn Fein, until its IRA guerrilla allies end their war against British rule.
He identifies himself with ordinary Irish people. He was christened Bartholemew Patrick Ahern but few of Ireland's 3.5 million people would know who that was. But they know Bertie.

They saw on their television sets in late 1994 a bitterly disappointed Finance Minister who felt he had been robbed of the prize of becoming prime minister when his predecessor, Albert Reynolds, quit in a row over legal appointments.
The prize went to his rival, John Bruton, leader of the Fine Gael party, who cobbled together a centre-left coalition which survived until Ireland's June 6 election and Ahern's win.
Friends say a subsequent spell in opposition helped the pugnacious parliamentary performer get to grips with party machinery, and smooth the edges of a raw personal image.
"It did him good. I don't think anyone ever doubted that he would get Fianna Fail back into government," said one long-time associate as Ahern celebrated at party headquarters.

Ahern's political handlers cast him as the voice of modern Ireland, a rapidly developing and prosperous state but one which is proud of its traditions and past and cherishes its uniqueness in what it sees as a homogenising Europe.
A devout but pragmatic Catholic, a young but experienced politician, Ahern promised something for everyone .
He pledged that the people of Ireland would enjoy the fruits of an unprecedented economic boom through a cut in the top rate of tax from 48 percent to 45 over the next five years.

Despite his relative youth, Ahern is a vastly experienced politician having served as labour minister, finance minister and even mayor of Dublin in a political career that began in 1977 when he was first elected to parliament.
Economic analysts have commended his handling of Ireland's devaluation crisis in January 1993, since when the economy, partly due to outside factors, has fared well.
Ahern is seen in the party as a protg of Charles Haughey, who was a Fianna Fail prime minister three times.
"He shares with his political mentor Charles Haughey a certain elusive charm and is comfortable with his Man-of-the-People image," one profiler said of the avid sports fan.

But Ahern quickly distanced himself from Haughey when a payments-to-politicians tribunal shortly before the election was told that the ex-premier was given more than a million pounds ($1.5 million) by tycoon Ben Dunne for unspecified purposes.

He also, friends say, did something about his dress sense. He was dubbed "anorak man" in his early days for his choice of casual attire but the double-breasted suit and artfully knotted tie have replaced all that.

Born in 1951 in the city's north side suburb of Drumcondra, he still lives there and has a powerful grass-roots party following and fund-raising machine in the city. He studied at Dublin's University College and the London School of Economics.

A Catholic who is conservative on social issues such as abortion, contraception and divorce, he nevertheless separated from his wife of 19 years, Miriam Kelly, blaming the stress of his job. But he still sees a lot of his two teenage daughters.
His public discussion of his marriage and his admission that he has a girlfriend is unusual for Irish politicians and a separated prime minister is unprecedented.
"He is every great Irish mother's son," the Irish Times said in 1993. "He may not wear odd socks but his oversized suits, slight stutter and constant gulping have endeared him to the public."
